t: Minimum Rectangles to Cover Points — Greedy on Sorted X
o: Rectangles are anchored to the x-axis with width at most w and unbounded height, so y-coordinates are irrelevant: a rectangle covers a set of points iff its x-span covers their x-coordinates. Sort the distinct x-coordinates and sweep greedily: start a rectangle at the leftmost uncovered x and extend it as far right as x ≤ start + w allows; repeat. Example 2 with w = 2 over x = 0..6 needs rectangles [0,2], [3,5], [6,6] → 3. This greedy is optimal because delaying a rectangle's start never covers more points.
k: Height is unlimited, so the problem reduces to covering sorted x-coordinates with intervals of length w.
Greedy: place each new rectangle's left edge at the first uncovered x.
Equivalent to counting groups of x-values within a sliding span of w.

a.i: Sort the unique x-coordinates. Maintain the left edge `cur` of the currently open rectangle; whenever the next x exceeds cur + w, close it, open a new one at that x, and increment the count.
s: Extract and sort distinct x values.
For each subsequent x: if x > cur + w, count++, cur = x.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting the x-coordinates dominates; the sweep is linear.

w: Exchange-argument proof: any optimal solution's leftmost rectangle can be shifted so its left edge is the smallest uncovered x without losing coverage. Pitfalls: forgetting duplicate x-values (harmless but wasteful), and w = 0 forcing one rectangle per distinct x. Follow-up: rectangles with bounded height too (then y matters and it becomes a harder covering problem), or streaming points.
